title: Fulfilment of Fibromyalgia Criteria and Concomitant Pain-Related Diagnoses in Patients Referred for or Labelled as Having Fibromyalgia: A Retrospective Cross-Sectional Pilot Study
content: Background/Objectives: Fibromyalgia (FM) is diagnosed using symptom-based criteria, and clinician-assigned labels may diverge from standardized classification frameworks. FM may also coexist with other pain-generating musculoskeletal disorders. We determined the proportion of patients referred for suspected or previously diagnosed FM who fulfilled the 2019 ACTTION-American Pain Society Pain Taxonomy (AAPT) criteria after specialist record-based adjudication and compared documented concomitant pain-related diagnoses and symptom severity according to AAPT status. Methods: This retrospective, single-center cross-sectional pilot study included consecutive adult outpatients evaluated in a tertiary pain unit for suspected or previously diagnosed FM. Routinely collected clinical records were reviewed to determine fulfilment of the AAPT 2019 criteria, identify documented concomitant pain-related diagnoses, and assess symptom severity using FIQR, Zung SAS/SDS, DN4, and NRS measures. Results: Among 76 patients (96.1% female), 28 fulfilled the AAPT criteria (36.8%; 95% CI, 26.9–48.1). Of these, 25 (89.3%; 95% CI, 72.8–96.3) had at least one documented concomitant pain-related diagnosis, compared with 26/48 (54.2%) patients who did not fulfil the criteria (OR, 7.05; 95% CI, 1.87–26.54; p = 0.002). Exploratory analyses showed higher FIQR, SAS, SDS, and DN4 scores in the AAPT MET group, whereas NRS pain intensity did not differ significantly. Conclusions: Approximately one-third of patients in this referral-based cohort fulfilled the AAPT criteria, and concomitant pain-related diagnoses were common. Because the retrospective adjudication, small single-center sample, and potential definitional and detection biases limit causal interpretation, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating. They suggest that criteria-based classification and clinical assessment provide complementary information when evaluating chronic widespread pain.
